newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan court recognises Ainu as indigenous people.
newsitem.headline: Japan court recognises Ainu as indigenous people.

text.p: A Japanese court for the first time formally recognised the Ainu people of northern Japan as an indigenous minority on Thursday and criticised national governments for having ignored their rights.

In a landmark ruling, Judge Kazuo Ichimiya of the Sapporo District Court said the state illegally expropriated land from two Ainu landowners to build a dam on Hokkaido, Japan's northernmost island where most Ainu live.
"The Ainu people, having inhabited mainly Hokkaido before the island came under our country's rule, have retained their originality and culture," Judge Ichimiya said.
"The state, although required to give full consideration for the culture of the Ainu race, unjustly ignored or belittled this (by expropriating land for the dam)," the judge said.

It was Japan's first court ruling which recognised that the Ainu, who have lived in northern Japan, Sakhalin and the Kurile Islands since prehistoric times, had legal rights protecting the preservation of their culture.

The plaintiffs, Upper House member of parliament Shigeru Kayano and farmer Koichi Kaizawa, filed a suit in 1993 demanding the state cancel a 1987 expropriation order on land they owned along a river sacred to the Ainu people.
Until construction of the dam, the Ainu annually conducted a religious rite for salmon -- their staple food -- along the banks of the Nibutani River.
Many Ainu archaeological and holy sites also dot the area.
The dam was completed last year.
Although ruling that the decision to expropriate Ainu land was illegal, Judge Ichimiya did not order the land be given back, saying the public benefit of the dam took precedence.
"Today's ruling is a giant step in our efforts to regain the rights of the Ainu people," Kayano, Japan's first and only Ainu member of parliament, told reporters after the ruling.
"We withhold comment," said Koji Hojo of the Hokkaido Development Agency, who represented the state in court. "We will refer the case to other related government agencies."
For centuries, Japanese traders and warriors massacred or exploited the Ainu, discriminating against them as primitive hunter-gatherers.
Since the 1868 Meiji Restoration, it was official Japanese policy to abolish the Ainu culture, banning the language and religious ceremonies.

Now numbering about 25,000, mainly on Hokkaido, the Ainu started a campaign to have their culture recognised in 1986 when former Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone told parliament Japan was a single-race country.
When Japan ratified the United Nations Human Rights Charter in 1979, the government reported to the U.N. that there was no minority race in Japan.
The government retracted the statement in 1991.

Earlier this month, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said his government will submit a new Ainu law to parliament to replace a century-old law that academics and activists say has long served to discriminate against Ainu.
